About

  • 🌏

    r @ y Olguin is a Research Engineering Technician with the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory (LPL). At HiROC, the operations center for NASA’s HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), he produces HiRISE and CTX DTMs, leads the HiRISE XR Development Program, and helps validate planetary datasets for NASA’s PDS with senior scientists at PSI.

  • 🌗

    From photon to pixel to planet: he builds high–resolution Digital Terrain Models of Mars through stereo alignment, bundle adjustment, orthorectification, and MOLA geodetic control, with sub–meter accuracy that supports surface–change studies, rover traverse planning, and mission design.

  • ⚡

    He is pursuing a B.S. in Electrical and Computer Engineering with an electrical engineering focus and minors in Planetary Science, Mathematics, Computer Engineering, and Italian. Training in project management, architectural and landscape design, and 3D/XR visualization places him at the intersection of satellite systems engineering and planetary science.

A Note on Exploration

That goal is not abstract. It was built one late night at a time, at a SOCET SET workstation, watching Mars resolve into terrain. In his own words:

"The most powerful systems I've worked on don't run on voltage or photon flux. They run on human curiosity. And America, at its best, has always been the place that refuses to waste it."
I've spent thousands of hours inside that pipeline. Extracting sub-pixel elevation data from Martian terrain, validating geodetic control against MOLA, delivering elevation models that support rover EDL targeting at NASA scale. Sitting alone at that workstation at 2am, watching a digital elevation model of Mars render line by line, I've felt something that has no engineering term for it. The weight of everyone who made that moment possible. Everyone who was told they didn't belong in that room and showed up anyway.
Read the full note
Every one of them sharpened the instrument. Every perspective we almost lost made the science smaller. Every engineer we found in a place nobody thought to look moved the mission forward.
And America keeps finding them. That is not accident. That is who we are at our best.
Europa Clipper is in flight right now. Artemis is building toward the Moon. The power architectures and flight instrumentation being designed in labs like mine will define the next fifty years of planetary science and the first chapter of permanent human presence beyond this world.
That story is not finished. It is accelerating.
The next generation of American engineers will carry it forward. All of them. From every corner of this country, every background, every frequency this nation holds. Not because it is the right thing to do. Because incomplete teams produce incomplete science, and we have too much left to discover to leave anyone behind.
The universe doesn't draw borders.
The best version of America never did either.
And the most powerful thing we will ever launch into deep space is the full signal. Every one of us, pointed at the same horizon.

Two Views, One Surface

Every DTM starts as two HiRISE images of the same ground, taken on different orbits. The emission angle is how far each view tilts from straight down; the incidence angle is how low the Sun sits. The two views must differ so the terrain shows parallax, and the Orthoimage cover uses the more vertical image of each pair, the one with the least geometric lean (McEwen et al., 2007; Kirk et al., 2008).

Viewing geometry

Image 1 looks almost straight down; image 2 is rolled off-nadir. The difference in viewpoint is what lets photogrammetry recover elevation.

Latitude alone does not set the angle: the south-polar zone holds both the most vertical view in the set (South Polar Deposits, 0.05°) and the two most oblique (20.1° and Cavi Angusti, 17.8°), while the equatorial sites have the highest median.

Science Experiment 017 · Topographic Modeling · Target: Europa
The storyline · Science Experiment 017

Goal. Turn Galileo DEMs into controlled test scenes with synthetic multiscale roughness, where every feature’s true shape, size, position and georeferenced location is known in advance, vertically and horizontally, so surface-detection and roughness-recovery methods can be validated against ground truth.

  1. 01PreprocessingGeoreferenced DEM rasters become Blender-ready meshes; data gaps kept, native roughness measured first.
  2. 02DEM_CropA parametric working window of any size, position and rotation, cut by ray projection with full provenance.
  3. 03RidgesSingle and double Europa ridges emplaced on terrain with Head (1999) cross-section profiles and FWHM widths.
  4. 04LenticulaePits and domes from Pappalardo (1998) morphometry, as a statistical scatter or exactly specified targets.
  5. 05PlumesCryovolcanic deposit fields: radial, directional or multi-lobed, with power-law clast sizes that decay from the vent.
  6. 06RoughnessHemispheres, pyramids, tetrahedra and polytopes scattered or excavated, realized vs requested against a 5M-face budget.

Objective. Turn Galileo DEMs into controlled test scenes with synthetic multiscale roughness, where every feature’s true shape, size, position, and georeferenced location is known in advance both vertically and horizontally, with EMILIA–3D’s stereo and thermal imaging of lunar regolith as an analog case, so surface–detection and roughness–recovery methods can be validated against ground truth.

6–tool terrain toolchain
01 Preprocessing

Convert georeferenced DEM rasters into Blender–ready meshes while preserving data gaps and measuring each terrain’s native roughness before any synthetic features are added.

02 DEM_Crop

Extract a parametric working window of any size, position, and rotation from a large DEM by ray projection, with full provenance stored on the output.

03 Ridges

Emplace single and double Europa ridges directly on terrain using Head (1999) cross–section profiles and FWHM widths.

04 Europa’s Lenticulae

Populate a DEM with pits and domes following Pappalardo (1998) morphometry, as a statistical scatter or as exactly specified targets.

05 Plumes

Model cryovolcanic plume deposit fields with radial, directional, or multi–lobed spread, finite range, and power–law clast sizing that decays with distance from the vent (still in development).

06 Roughness

Scatter or excavate instanced hemispheres, pyramids, tetrahedra, and convex polytopes with independent control of density, coverage, size, height, and orientation, reporting realized versus requested populations against a 5M face computational budget.

Zones of Mars, Two Ways of Seeing

One site per latitude zone, pole to pole. Each pairs the orthoimage (what HiRISE saw) with color altimetry (what the DTM measured), co-registered from their PDS map labels. Drag across each image: the same landform read two ways explains a different chapter of Mars’ history, and the emission angle shows how directly HiRISE could look down at each latitude (Kirk et al., 2008; McEwen et al., 2007; Sutton et al., 2022).

Bench scarps expose ice and dust layers accumulated over millions of years of obliquity-paced climate cycles. In the orthoimage the layers are bright and dark bands; in the altimetry each band becomes a measurable step, so layer thickness can be read in metres. A near-vertical view keeps the thin layers undistorted (Byrne, 2009; Fishbaugh et al., 2010; Laskar et al., 2002).

PSP_010109_2655 · 165.6°E · Elevation ramp spans the 1st–99th percentile of the image shown; shading uses 2.5× vertical exaggeration, colours are true elevation (Kirk et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2022).

Lobate debris aprons and lineated valley fill along the dichotomy boundary are remnants of Late Amazonian debris-covered glaciers. The orthoimage shows the flow lineations; the altimetry shows the downslope gradient they follow, the signature of viscous ice flow under a protective debris cover (Head et al., 2010; Plaut et al., 2009).

ESP_049621_2210 · 47.9°E · Elevation ramp spans the 1st–99th percentile of the image shown; shading uses 2.5× vertical exaggeration, colours are true elevation (Kirk et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2022).

Uranius Mons is a shield volcano in northeastern Tharsis. The altimetry measures crater depth and rim height against the shield’s gentle flank slope; morphometry of this kind (height, slope, crater dimensions) is how Martian volcanoes are compared with one another (Kirk et al., 2008; Plescia, 2004).

ESP_067495_2080 · 271.0°E · Elevation ramp spans the 1st–99th percentile of the image shown; shading uses 2.5× vertical exaggeration, colours are true elevation (Kirk et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2022).

Hebes Mensa is the interior layered deposit of a closed trough in the Valles Marineris system, among the thickest sedimentary sequences on Mars. The full DTM spans 2,970 m of relief, the most in the portfolio; the altimetry shows how steeply the eroded layer benches step down (Kirk et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2018).

ESP_017319_1785 · 284.8°E · Elevation ramp spans the 1st–99th percentile of the image shown; shading uses 2.5× vertical exaggeration, colours are true elevation (Kirk et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2022).

Pits in a vanished ice sheet

Cavi Angusti · Polar & Ice

Cavi Angusti are steep-walled pits up to about a kilometre deep, cut into the Hesperian Dorsa Argentea Formation, which is interpreted as the deposit of a former south circumpolar ice sheet that melted and retreated. The most vertical image available here was 17.75° off nadir; orthorectification uses the DTM to remove that lean, so every feature still sits at its true map position (Dickson & Head, 2006; Head & Pratt, 2001; Kirk et al., 2008).

ESP_013720_1035 · 283.5°E · Elevation ramp spans the 1st–99th percentile of the image shown; shading uses 2.5× vertical exaggeration, colours are true elevation (Kirk et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2022).

How to read these pairs

Brightness is not height

An orthoimage records how much sunlight each patch reflects: tone mixes albedo, frost, dust and slope shading, so a dark band can be a low trough or just darker material. Color altimetry removes that ambiguity: every colour is a measured elevation from the stereo DTM, on the scale under each image (Fishbaugh et al., 2010; Kirk et al., 2008; McEwen et al., 2007).

The emission angle of the best view depends on how each target was scheduled, not simply on latitude: the five zones below range from 0.37° to 17.75°. Orthorectification uses the DTM to correct the lean either way (Kirk et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2022).

Temporal baselines are estimated from the MRO orbit numbers in each HiRISE product ID at about 12.9 orbits per Earth day (≈112 min period), so elapsed times are approximate. Long baselines flag pairs where surface change between images (frost, mass wasting, dune migration) can affect stereo correlation and are candidates for dedicated change-detection work. MRO orbit geometry follows Zurek & Smrekar (2007); documented present-day activity at gully, dune, and polar sites follows Dundas et al. (2012), Bridges et al. (2012), and Byrne (2009).
